Profile of the Economy 
 [Source: Office of Macroeconomic Analysis] 
As of November 6, 2015 
 
Introduction 
Growth of real gross domestic product (GDP) slowed in 
the third quarter of 2015, largely due to a marked pullback in 
the pace of inventory investment. However, other 
components of real GDP continued to grow at a solid pace. 
Labor market conditions continued to improve, and the 
unemployment rate declined to 5.0 percent in October, its 
lowest level since April 2008. Inflation remained low, in part 
reflecting the steep decline in energy prices since mid-2014. 
Despite some fluctuations, energy prices remained well-
below year-ago levels as of early November. 
The Administration has taken a number of steps in recent 
years to promote stronger economic growth in the near term, 
but has also pursued deficit reduction measures in the 
interests of the nation’s longer-term growth. Since 2011, the 
budget deficit has been reduced by more than $4 trillion 
(including the deep cuts imposed by sequestration). The 
federal budget deficit has fallen from a peak of 9.8 percent 
of GDP in fiscal year 2009 to 2.5 percent in fiscal year 2015, 
and is expected to fall slightly further on net in the coming 
fiscal years. 
At its most recent meeting in October 2015, the Federal 
Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) 
announced it would maintain the target range for the federal 
funds rate of 0 to 0.25 percent as well as existing programs 
for reinvestment of principal payments and roll-overs of 
maturing Treasuries at auction. The Committee also 
observed that it “anticipates that it will be appropriate to 
raise the target range for the federal funds rate when it has 
seen further improvement in the labor market and is 
reasonably confident that inflation will move back to its 2 
percent objective over the medium term.” 
Economic Growth 
Since the current expansion began in mid-2009, the 
economy has grown by 14.2 percent and, as of the third 
quarter of 2015, real GDP was 9.4 percent above its level at 
the end of 2007, when the recession began. According to the 
advance estimate, real GDP rose 1.5 percent at an annual 
rate during the third quarter of 2015, after advancing 3.9 
percent in the second quarter. Consumer spending growth 
decelerated somewhat in the third quarter, but was still 
relatively strong and made a substantial contribution to 
overall GDP growth. Residential investment grew solidly in 
the third quarter, if at a slower pace than in the second, and 
made a small positive contribution to real GDP growth. 
Business fixed investment also grew, as growth in 
equipment investment and spending on intellectual property 
products helped offset a pull-back in structures investment. 
Federal Government outlays rose in the third quarter as did 
State and local government spending, although the latter 
grew at a slower pace. Overall, the government sector 
provided a small boost to growth in the third quarter. The 
trade deficit widened slightly, as export growth slowed, but 
net exports were essentially neutral for third-quarter GDP 
growth, after making a small positive contribution in the 
second quarter. In contrast, private inventory accumulation 
slowed sharply, holding back overall growth by a substantial 
amount. 
Private domestic final demand (consumption plus private 
fixed investment, considered a better measure of underlying 
private demand because it subtracts out government 
spending, inventory movements, and net exports) grew at a 
3.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, following a 3.9 
percent increase in the second quarter. Real personal 
consumption expenditures—which account for about 68 
percent of GDP—rose at a 3.2 percent annual rate in the 
third quarter, moderating somewhat from a 3.6 percent pace 
in the second quarter. Altogether, consumption contributed 
2.2 percentage points to real GDP growth in the third 
quarter. 
Housing activity has stepped up over the past year. 
Residential investment—mostly residential home-building—
advanced 6.1 percent at an annual rate in the third quarter, 
following a 9.1 percent jump in the second quarter. 
Residential activity accounts for just 3 percent of GDP, and 
added 0.2 percentage point to third-quarter real GDP growth. 

4 
PROFILE OF THE ECONOMY 
December 2015 
Home building and home sales remain on a gradual 
upward trend. New residential construction activity has 
recovered from weather-related regional slowdowns in early 
2015 and advanced 12.0 percent over the year through 
September 2015 to an annual rate of 740,000 units. Even so, 
single-family starts remain more than 59 percent below their 
January 2006 peak, and well below the 1.1 million unit 
average observed from 1980 to 2004. In contrast, multi-
family starts are well above their pre-recession level. Sales 
of new single-family homes rose 2.0 percent over the year 
through September to a 468,000 annual rate. Sales of all 
existing homes (94 percent of all home sales, including 
single-family, condos and co-ops) rose 8.8 percent over the 
year to just over 5.5 million at an annual rate in September 
2015. 
Household formation—a key determinant of demand for 
new housing—has risen to a much stronger level in recent 
quarters, providing support to overall housing activity. In the 
year through the third quarter of 2015, nearly 1.5 million 
households were formed, roughly twice the pace observed in

recent years and  well above the long-term average of 1.3 
million recorded from 1966 to 2007. 
Home prices have continued to rise, although the pace of 
increase has moderated from the rapid pace observed in mid-
2013. The FHFA purchase-only home price index rose 5.5 
percent over the year ending in August 2015, down from the 
July 2013 peak rate of 8.1 percent. The Standard and Poor’s 
(S&P)/Case-Shiller composite 20-city home price index rose 
5.1 percent over the year ending in August 2015, down from 
a peak of 13.7 percent in November 2013. Other house price 
measures show a similar pattern of decelerating home price 
appreciation. 
Growth of nonresidential fixed investment—about 13 
percent of GDP—grew by 2.1 percent at an annual rate in 
the third quarter of 2015, following a 4.1 percent increase in 
the second quarter. Growth of equipment investment 
accelerated to 5.3 percent in the third quarter from a modest 
0.3 percent gain in the previous quarter. In contrast, business 
spending on intellectual property products—including 
outlays for software, research and development, and 
entertainment, literary and artistic originals—slowed to a 1.8 
percent pace from 8.3 percent in the second quarter. In 
addition, business outlays for structures fell 4.0 percent. 
Altogether, nonresidential fixed investment added 0.3 
percentage point to real GDP growth in the third quarter, 
after making a 0.5 percentage point contribution in the 
second quarter. Finally, businesses accumulated inventories 
at a markedly slower pace in the third quarter following a 
substantial run-up earlier in the year. The resulting change in 
private inventories subtracted 1.4 percentage points from 
third-quarter real GDP growth. 
Exports account for about 13 percent of GDP, while 
imports (which are subtracted from total domestic spending 
to calculate GDP) account for just over 16 percent. In the 
third quarter of 2015, exports grew 1.9 percent. However, 
the small rise in exports was roughly offset by a 1.8 percent 
increase in imports. As a result, the net export deficit was 
little changed in the third quarter compared with its second-
quarter average and had a negligible impact on real GDP 
growth. Net exports added 0.2 percentage point to GDP 
growth in the second quarter after subtracting nearly 2 
percentage points from growth in the first quarter of 2015. 
The current account balance (reflecting international 
trade in goods and services as well as investment income 
flows and unilateral transfers) has been in deficit almost 
continuously since the early 1980s and in 2006 reached a 
record $807 billion, equivalent to 5.8 percent of GDP. The 
current account deficit narrowed sharply during the 
recession to $384 billion (2.6 percent of GDP) in 2009. It 
has widened somewhat since then but remains well below its 
2006 peak. In 2014, the current account deficit stood at $390 
billion, or 2.2 percent of GDP. In the second quarter of 2015, 
the current account deficit widened to $439 billion 
(annualized), or 2.5 percent of GDP. 
Government purchases—which account for about 18 
percent of GDP—have contributed modestly on net to 
economic growth thus far in 2015 after subtracting from 
GDP growth in each of the past 4 years. In the third quarter, 
government outlays advanced 1.7 percent at an annual rate 
after growing 2.6 percent in the second quarter. At the 
federal level, spending increased by 0.3 percent after a flat 
reading in the second quarter. State and local government 
spending rose by 2.6 percent following a 4.3 percent 
advance in the second quarter. State and local government 
spending declined for 14 straight quarters from the fourth 
quarter of 2009 through the first quarter of 2013-the longest 
period of falling expenditures at this level of government in 
postwar history-but has risen almost continuously since the 
first quarter of 2013. Similarly, spending cutbacks at the 
federal level restrained overall growth from 2011 through 
2014. 
Labor Markets 
During the recession (from December 2007 through June 
2009), the economy lost 7.4 million jobs. Job losses 
continued even after the recovery began, but in February 
2010 employment began to rise again. Since then, through 
October 2015, total nonfarm payroll employment has 
increased by 13.0 million. Private-sector employment has 
grown for 68 consecutive months, the longest string of 
increases on record, and has risen by almost 13.5 million. 
Job losses during the recession were spread broadly 
across most sectors but, with the resumption of job growth, 
all of these sectors have added jobs. Since the labor market 
recovery began in early 2010, payrolls in professional and 
business services have risen by nearly 3.4 million, and the 
leisure and hospitality industry’s employment has increased 
by almost 2.4 million through October 2015. Employment in 
the manufacturing sector has expanded by 864,000 since 
early 2010. A few sectors added jobs throughout the 
recession and still continue to hire new workers: since early 
2010, the health care and social assistance sector has added 

PROFILE OF THE ECONOMY 
5 
December 2015 
an additional 2.1 million jobs. On a net basis, the 
government sector also added workers to payrolls during the 
recession, although payrolls began declining late in 2008, 
and 
trended 
lower 
until 
early 
2014. 
Government 
employment has increased since then but growth has been 
uneven. From early 2014 through October 2015, the 
government sector has added just 177,000 jobs. Most of the 
growth has occurred at the local level, with the addition of 
124,000 positions. Federal government employment has 
edged up just 2,000 during this period. 
The unemployment rate peaked in October 2009 at a 26-
year high of 10.0 percent—5.4 percentage points above the 
4.6 percent average that prevailed in 2006 and 2007, before 
the recession began. Since then, the unemployment rate has 
trended lower and in October 2015 stood at 5.0 percent. 
Broader measures of unemployment have also declined. The 
broadest measure, which includes workers who are 
underemployed as well as those who are only marginally 
attached to the labor force (the U-6 unemployment rate), has 
fallen from a record high of 17.1 percent in early 2010 to 9.8 
percent in October 2015. The U-6 unemployment rate is still 
above its pre-recession average of 8.3 percent. The 
percentage of the unemployed who have been out of work 
for 27 weeks or more also remains elevated relative to its 
pre-recession average. In October, 26.8 percent of 
unemployed workers were included in this category 
compared with readings around 17.5 percent before the 
recession. 
Inflation 
Headline and core inflation rates remained relatively low 
and stable, due in part to low energy prices. Headline 
consumer prices were unchanged over the 12 months ending 
in September 2015, after rising 1.7 percent over the same 
period a year earlier. Energy prices fell 18.4 percent in the 
year through September 2015, substantially more than the 
0.6 percent decline in the year through September 2014. 
Food prices rose 1.6 percent over the year through 
September 2015, slowing from the 3.0 percent increase over 
the 12 months ending in September 2014. On a 12-month 
basis, core consumer prices (a measure that excludes food 
and energy) rose 1.9 percent through September 2015, 
slightly faster than the 1.7 percent advance in the year 
through September 2014. Core inflation has been below 2 
percent since early 2013. 
Oil and gasoline prices fell sharply between mid-2014 
and early 2015. They trended higher in the spring and early 
summer but have generally declined since then and remain 
well below their year-earlier levels. The front-month futures 
price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil averaged 
$46.29 per barrel in October 2015, more than $38 below its 
October 2014 average. The retail price of regular gasoline 
averaged $2.23 per gallon in October 2015, 83 cents lower 
than in October 2014. 
Federal Budget and Debt 
The federal budget deficit declined to $439 billion (2.5 
percent of GDP) in fiscal year 2015 from $483 billion (2.8 
percent of GDP) in fiscal year 2014. The deficit has 
declined by 7.3 percentage points from a peak of 9.8 percent 
in fiscal year 2009, and is now at its lowest level since fiscal 
year 2007. Debt held by the public rose to $13.1 trillion in 
fiscal year 2015. As a share of the economy, publicly held 
debt declined from 74.4 percent of GDP at the end of fiscal 
year 2014 to 73.8 percent at the end of fiscal year 2015. 
In February 2015, the Administration released its 
Fiscal Year 2016 Budget, which is projected to lower the 
budget deficit slightly further in the near term and put the 

6 
PROFILE OF THE ECONOMY 
December 2015 
debt-to-GDP ratio on a declining path. The latest budget 
proposal would replace sequestration with targeted spending 
cuts and loophole closures, pay for all new investments, and 
achieve an additional $1.8 trillion in deficit reduction over 
the 10-year budget horizon. Deficit reduction would be 
achieved primarily through reforms to health programs, the 
tax code, and immigration. Updated projections in the Mid-
Session Review of the Fiscal Year 2016 Budget show the 
federal budget narrowing to 2.2 percent of GDP by fiscal 
year 2017 and stabilizing at 2.7 percent of GDP in the latter 
half of the 10-year budget window. The debt-to-GDP ratio is 
projected to stabilize at 74.6 percent of GDP in fiscal year 
2018 and remain at that level through the end of the 10-year 
forecast horizon. The primary deficit is projected to become 
a primary surplus in fiscal year 2024, at which point it will 
no longer be adding to federal debt. 
Economic Policy 
Key fiscal and monetary policy actions taken over the 
past few years have aided the recovery. On the fiscal policy 
side, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) 
of 2009 authorized the Federal Government to spend $787 
billion to stimulate domestic demand, an amount that was 
increased to $840 billion to be consistent with the 
President’s Fiscal Year 2012 Budget. This spending 
provided an important boost to economic activity, but the 
Administration also proposed and implemented a variety of 
additional programs to maintain the recovery’s momentum. 
These included an extension and expansion of the first-time 
home buyer tax credit, a new Small Business Jobs and 
Wages Tax Credit, and additional financial support for State 
and local Governments. In December 2010, the 2010 Tax 
Relief Act authorized a 2 percentage point payroll tax cut, 
extensions of unemployment benefits and refundable tax 
credits, and a 2-year extension of the 2001 tax cuts. In late 
December 2011, the 2 percentage point payroll tax cut and 
extended unemployment benefits included in the 2010 tax 
legislation were each extended for 2 additional months. In 
late February 2012, the extension of the payroll tax cut and 
extended unemployment benefits for the remainder of 2012 
were signed into law. 
In January 2013, the ATRA was signed into law. The 
American 
Taxpayer 
Relief 
Act 
of 
2012 
(ATRA) 
permanently extended tax cuts for the vast majority of 
Americans and small businesses, extended Emergency 
Unemployment benefits for an additional year, extended a 
variety of other tax cuts and credits, postponed the sequester, 
originally scheduled to take effect on January 1, until March 
1, 2013, and raised tax rates for high-income earners 
(representing about 2 percent of taxpayers). Altogether, the 
ATRA is projected to reduce the deficit by $737 billion over 
the next decade. 
Partly in response to rising financial market stress, as 
well as to signs of more slowing in the broader economy, the 
Federal Reserve began the current cycle of monetary policy 
easing in September 2007. By late 2008, the FOMC had 
lowered the federal funds target interest rate dramatically, 
reducing it to a historically low range of 0 to 0.25 percent at 
the December 2008 FOMC meeting. Beginning with the 
August 2011 meeting, the FOMC also began identifying an 
expected timeframe for maintaining the federal funds rate 
target at “exceptionally low levels.” Initially put at mid-
2013, the timeframe was extended to “at least late 2014” at 
the January 2012 FOMC meeting, and then to “at least mid-
2015” at the September 2012 meeting, a timeframe for the 
target range which was maintained at the October 2012 
meeting. At the December 2012 meeting, the FOMC 
implemented numerical thresholds for its policy rate 
guidance. Specifically, the FOMC indicated that it would 
maintain the target range at least as long as the 
unemployment rate remained above 6.5 percent, inflation 
between 1 and 2 years ahead is projected to be no more than 
0.5 percentage point above the FOMC’s 2 percent longer-run 
goal, and long-term inflation expectations remain well 
anchored. At the December 2013 meeting, the FOMC 
commented on the role of the numerical thresholds in 
formulating monetary policy, indicating that, “it will likely 
be appropriate to maintain the current target range for the 
federal funds rate well past the time that the unemployment 
rate declines below 6-½ percent, especially if projected 
inflation continues to run below the Committee’s longer run 
goal.” At the FOMC meeting in March 2014, the Committee 
replaced the numerical thresholds in favor of qualitative 
guidance, noting it will “assess progress-both realized and 
expected-towards its objectives of maximum employment 
and 2 percent inflation” and that, “it will likely be 
appropriate to maintain the current target range … for a 
considerable time after the asset purchase program ends, 
especially if projected inflation continues to run below the 
Committee’s 2 percent longer-run goal, and provided longer-
term inflation expectations remain well anchored.”

maintained the qualitative forward guidance adopted at the 
March 2014 FOMC meeting and also left out any reference to

also repeated its view, first expressed at the March 2015 
meeting, that, “it will be appropriate to raise the target range 
for the federal funds rate when it has seen further 
improvement in the labor market and is reasonably confident 
that inflation will move back to its 2 percent objective over 
the medium term.” At its April 2015 meeting, the FOMC had 
added “import prices” to the range of information it assesses 
in determining monetary policy, and in July, September, and 
October, the Committee maintained previous references to 
energy and non-energy import prices.

768:securities into the latter securities. At the June 2012 meeting, 
769:the FOMC extended and expanded its program to extend the 
770:average maturity of its holdings (the so-called “twist” 
771:operation announced in September 2011). At the September 
772:2012 meeting, the FOMC announced it would increase 
773:monetary accommodation through $40 billion per month in 
774:additional purchases of mortgage-backed securities through 
775:the end of the year. The FOMC announced additional 
776:monetary accommodation at the December 2012 meeting, 
777:including the completion of short-term securities sales 
778:(which drain liquidity) and the continuation of purchases of 
779:long-term Treasury securities at a rate of $45 billion per 
780:month beyond the end of 2012. The FOMC also indicated 
781:that monthly purchases of mortgage-backed securities at a 
782:pace of $40 billion per month would continue, and affirmed 
783:its existing policy of reinvesting principal payments. 
784:At the December 2013 meeting, the FOMC announced a 
785:tapering of long-term Treasury security purchases and 
786:mortgage-backed securities purchases of $5 billion each, 
787:beginning in January 2014. The tapering brought monthly 
788:purchases to $40 billion and $35 billion, respectively. At 
789:each subsequent meeting in January, March, April, June, 
790:July, and September 2014, the Committee announced further 
791:tapering of asset purchases of $5 billion in each category. At 
792:its meeting in October 2014, the Committee announced the 
793:conclusion of its asset purchase program at the end of 
794:October 2014. 
795:Financial Markets 
796:Financial markets have largely recovered from the 
797:unprecedented strains experienced in the fall of 2008. Credit 
798:flows have increased substantially, although in the third 
799:quarter of 2015, fewer banks continued to ease standards and 
800:terms across a variety of lending categories. Nonetheless, 
801:measures of risk tolerance and volatility have all improved. 
802:Equity markets have more than recovered from the steep 
803:losses incurred in 2008, and volatility has declined 
804:markedly. The S&P 500 index, which in 2008 suffered its 
805:largest annual loss since the Great Depression, has increased 
806:2.0 percent so far this year and is currently about 31 percent 
807:above its October 2007 peak. The S&P Stock Market 
808:Volatility Index (VIX), often used as a measure of financial 
809:market uncertainty, stood at 15 as of early November 
810:2015—down sharply from an all-time high of 81 in 
811:November 2008. 
812:A variety of factors have buffeted long-term Treasury 
813:interest rates over the past several years, including flight-to-
814:quality flows in response to a variety of specific risk events, 
815:as well as supply concerns related to funding of the 
816:Government’s debt, and more recently, concerns about 
817:global financial markets and slowing global growth. The 
818:yield on the 10-year note has fluctuated around the 2 percent 
819:level during 2015, remaining well above the record low of 
820:1.43 percent reached in late July 2012. Currently, the 10-
821:year yield is 17 basis points higher on the year at 2.34 
822:percent, after falling by nearly 90 basis points in 2014. The 
823:3-month Treasury bill yield has fluctuated under 0.1 percent 
824:since January 2012, where it stood as of early November 
825:2015. The 2- to 10-year Treasury yield spread, one measure 
826:of the steepness of the yield curve, has been narrowing 
827:significantly since November 2013 and stood at about 144 
828:basis points as of early November 2015. 
829:Key interest rates on private securities, which spiked in 
830:response to financial market turbulence in late 2008, have 
831:since retraced as conditions have stabilized. The spread 
832:between the 3-month London Inter-bank Offered Rate 
833:(LIBOR) and the 3-month Treasury bill rate (also known as 
834:the TED spread, a measure of inter-bank liquidity and credit 
835:risk) rose to an all-time high of nearly 460 basis points in 
836:early October 2008. However, improvements in short-term 
837:credit availability have led to a narrowing of this spread, 
838:which stood at 29 basis points as of early November 2015. 
839:The spread between the Baa corporate bond yield and the 
840:10-year Treasury yield peaked at nearly 620 basis points in 
841:December 2008. The Baa-10-year spread had narrowed to 
842:213 basis points in April 2014, but thereafter, has widened

847:very gradually to 317 basis points, still very high by 
848:historical standards. 
849:Rates for conforming mortgages have trended lower in 
850:recent years, as have rates for jumbo mortgages. The interest 
851:rate for a 30-year conforming fixed-rate mortgage fell to a 
852:record low of 3.31 percent in November 2012. In the spring 
853:of 2013, however, it moved sharply higher, peaking at 4.58 
854:percent in August 2013. Since then, this rate has eased on 
855:net and in October 2015 averaged 3.78 percent. 
856:Foreign Exchange Rates 
857:The value of the U.S. dollar compared with the 
858:currencies of seven major trading partners (the euro area 
859:countries, Japan, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, 
860:Sweden, and Switzerland) appreciated to a peak level in 
861:February 2002, and then depreciated significantly over the 
862:next several years. From its peak in February 2002, to the 
863:recent low reached in August 2011, the exchange value of 
864:the dollar compared to an index of these currencies fell by 
865:about 39 percent. Although the dollar’s exchange value 
866:against this index remains well below the February 2002 
867:peak, it has appreciated between August 2011 and October 
868:2015 by about 32 percent. From August 2011 through 
869:October 2015, the dollar has appreciated by about 56 percent 
870:against the yen and by about 28 percent against the euro. 
871:Against an index of currencies of 19 other important trading 
872:partners (including China, India, and Mexico), the dollar has 
873:appreciated by about 20 percent.

880:INTRODUCTION: Federal Fiscal Operations 
881:Budget 
882:authority 
883:usually 
884:takes 
885:the 
886:form 
887:of 
888:appropriations that allow obligations to be incurred and 
889:payments to be made. Reappropriations are Congressional 
890:actions that extend the availability of unobligated amounts 
891:that have expired or would otherwise expire. These are 
892:counted as new budget authority in the fiscal year of the 
893:legislation in which the reappropriation act is included, 
894:regardless of when the amounts were originally appropriated 
895:or when they would otherwise lapse. 
896:Obligations generally are liquidated by the issuance of 
897:checks or the disbursement of cash—outlays. Obligations 
898:may also be liquidated (and outlays recorded) by the accrual 
899:of interest on public issues of Treasury debt securities 
900:(including an increase in redemption value of bonds 
901:outstanding); or by the issuance of bonds, debentures, notes, 
902:monetary credits, or electronic payments. 
903:Refunds of collections generally are treated as 
904:reductions of collections, whereas payments for earned-
905:income tax credits in excess of tax liabilities are treated as 
906:outlays. Outlays during a fiscal year may be for payment of 
907:obligations incurred in prior years or in the same year. 
908:Outlays, therefore, flow in part from unexpended balances 
909:of prior year budget authority and from budget authority 
910:provided for the year in which the money is spent. Total 
911:outlays include both budget and off-budget outlays and are 
912:stated net of offsetting collections. 
913:Receipts are reported in the tables as either budget 
914:receipts or offsetting collections. They are collections from 
915:the public, excluding receipts offset against outlays. These, 
916:also called governmental receipts, consist mainly of tax 
917:receipts (including social insurance taxes), receipts from 
918:court fines, certain licenses, and deposits of earnings by the 
919:Federal Reserve system. Refunds of receipts are treated as 
920:deductions from gross receipts. Total Government receipts 
921:are compared with total outlays in calculating the budget 
922:surplus or deficit. 
923:Offsetting collections from other Government accounts 
924:or the public are of a business-type or market-oriented 
925:nature. They are classified as either collections credited to 
926:appropriations or fund accounts, or offsetting receipts (i.e., 
927:amounts deposited in receipt accounts). The former 
928:normally can be used without an appropriation act by 
929:Congress. These occur in two instances: (1) when 
930:authorized by law, amounts collected for materials or 
931:services are treated as reimbursements to appropriations. 
932:For accounting purposes, earned reimbursements are also 
933:known as revenues. These offsetting collections are netted 
934:against gross outlays in determining net outlays from such 
935:appropriations; and (2) in the three types of revolving funds 
936:(public enterprise, intragovernmental, and trust); offsetting 
937:collections are netted against spending, and outlays are 
938:reported as the net amount. 
939:Offsetting receipts in receipt accounts cannot be used 
940:without appropriation. They are subdivided into three 
941:categories: (1) proprietary receipts, or collections from the 
942:public, offset against outlays by agency and by function; (2) 
943:intragovernmental transactions, or payments into receipt 
944:accounts from governmental appropriation or fund accounts. 
945:They finance operations within and between Government 
946:agencies and are credited with collections from other 
947:Government accounts; and (3) offsetting governmental 
948:receipts that include foreign cash contributions. 
949:Intrabudgetary transactions are subdivided into three 
950:categories: (1) interfund transactions—payments are from 
951:one fund group (either Federal funds or trust funds) to a 
952:receipt account in the other fund group; (2) Federal 
953:intrafund transactions—payments and receipts both occur 
954:within the Federal fund group; and (3) trust intrafund 
955:transactions—payments and receipts both occur within the 
956:trust fund group. 
957:Offsetting receipts are generally deducted from budget 
958:authority and outlays by function, subfunction, or agency. 
959:There are four types of receipts, however, that are deducted 
960:from budget totals as undistributed offsetting receipts. They 
961:are: (1) agencies’ payments (including payments by off-
962:budget Federal entities) as employers into employees’ 
963:retirement funds; (2) interest received by trust funds; (3) 
964:rents and royalties on the Outer Continental Shelf lands; and 
965:(4) other interest (i.e., that collected on Outer Continental 
966:Shelf money in deposit funds when such money is 
967:transferred into the budget). 
968:The Government has used the unified budget concept set 
969:forth in the “Report of the President’s Commission on 
970:Budget Concepts” as a foundation for its budgetary analysis 
971:and presentation since 1969. The concept calls for the 
972:budget to include all of the Government’s fiscal transactions 
973:with the public. Since 1971, however, various laws have 
974:been enacted removing several Federal entities from (or 
975:creating them outside of) the budget. Other laws have 
976:moved certain off-budget Federal entities onto the budget. 
977:Under current law, the off-budget Federal entities consist of 
978:the two Social Security trust funds, Federal Old-Age and 
979:Survivors Insurance and the Federal Disability Insurance 
980:Trust Fund, and the Postal Service.

361:Introduction 
362:Growth of real gross domestic product (GDP) slowed in 
363:the third quarter of 2015, largely due to a marked pullback in 
364:the pace of inventory investment. However, other 
365:components of real GDP continued to grow at a solid pace. 
366:Labor market conditions continued to improve, and the 
367:unemployment rate declined to 5.0 percent in October, its 
368:lowest level since April 2008. Inflation remained low, in part 
369:reflecting the steep decline in energy prices since mid-2014. 
370:Despite some fluctuations, energy prices remained well-
371:below year-ago levels as of early November. 
372:The Administration has taken a number of steps in recent 
373:years to promote stronger economic growth in the near term, 
374:but has also pursued deficit reduction measures in the 
375:interests of the nation’s longer-term growth. Since 2011, the 
376:budget deficit has been reduced by more than $4 trillion 
377:(including the deep cuts imposed by sequestration). The 
378:federal budget deficit has fallen from a peak of 9.8 percent 
379:of GDP in fiscal year 2009 to 2.5 percent in fiscal year 2015, 
380:and is expected to fall slightly further on net in the coming 
381:fiscal years. 
382:At its most recent meeting in October 2015, the Federal 
383:Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) 
384:announced it would maintain the target range for the federal 
385:funds rate of 0 to 0.25 percent as well as existing programs 
386:for reinvestment of principal payments and roll-overs of 
387:maturing Treasuries at auction. The Committee also 
388:observed that it “anticipates that it will be appropriate to 
389:raise the target range for the federal funds rate when it has 
390:seen further improvement in the labor market and is 
391:reasonably confident that inflation will move back to its 2 
392:percent objective over the medium term.” 
393:Economic Growth 
394:Since the current expansion began in mid-2009, the 
395:economy has grown by 14.2 percent and, as of the third 
396:quarter of 2015, real GDP was 9.4 percent above its level at 
397:the end of 2007, when the recession began. According to the 
398:advance estimate, real GDP rose 1.5 percent at an annual 
399:rate during the third quarter of 2015, after advancing 3.9 
400:percent in the second quarter. Consumer spending growth 
401:decelerated somewhat in the third quarter, but was still 
402:relatively strong and made a substantial contribution to 
403:overall GDP growth. Residential investment grew solidly in 
404:the third quarter, if at a slower pace than in the second, and 
405:made a small positive contribution to real GDP growth. 
406:Business fixed investment also grew, as growth in 
407:equipment investment and spending on intellectual property 
408:products helped offset a pull-back in structures investment. 
409:Federal Government outlays rose in the third quarter as did 
410:State and local government spending, although the latter 
411:grew at a slower pace. Overall, the government sector 
412:provided a small boost to growth in the third quarter. The 
413:trade deficit widened slightly, as export growth slowed, but 
414:net exports were essentially neutral for third-quarter GDP 
415:growth, after making a small positive contribution in the 
416:second quarter. In contrast, private inventory accumulation 
417:slowed sharply, holding back overall growth by a substantial 
418:amount. 
419:Private domestic final demand (consumption plus private 
420:fixed investment, considered a better measure of underlying 
421:private demand because it subtracts out government 
422:spending, inventory movements, and net exports) grew at a 
423:3.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, following a 3.9 
424:percent increase in the second quarter. Real personal 
425:consumption expenditures—which account for about 68 
426:percent of GDP—rose at a 3.2 percent annual rate in the 
427:third quarter, moderating somewhat from a 3.6 percent pace 
428:in the second quarter. Altogether, consumption contributed 
429:2.2 percentage points to real GDP growth in the third 
430:quarter. 
431:Housing activity has stepped up over the past year. 
432:Residential investment—mostly residential home-building—
433:advanced 6.1 percent at an annual rate in the third quarter, 
434:following a 9.1 percent jump in the second quarter. 
435:Residential activity accounts for just 3 percent of GDP, and 
436:added 0.2 percentage point to third-quarter real GDP growth. 
437:
438:4 
439:PROFILE OF THE ECONOMY 
440:December 2015 
441:Home building and home sales remain on a gradual 
442:upward trend. New residential construction activity has 
443:recovered from weather-related regional slowdowns in early 
444:2015 and advanced 12.0 percent over the year through 
445:September 2015 to an annual rate of 740,000 units. Even so, 
446:single-family starts remain more than 59 percent below their 
447:January 2006 peak, and well below the 1.1 million unit 
448:average observed from 1980 to 2004. In contrast, multi-
449:family starts are well above their pre-recession level. Sales 
450:of new single-family homes rose 2.0 percent over the year 
451:through September to a 468,000 annual rate. Sales of all 
452:existing homes (94 percent of all home sales, including 
453:single-family, condos and co-ops) rose 8.8 percent over the 
454:year to just over 5.5 million at an annual rate in September 
455:2015. 
456:Household formation—a key determinant of demand for 
457:new housing—has risen to a much stronger level in recent 
458:quarters, providing support to overall housing activity. In the 
459:year through the third quarter of 2015, nearly 1.5 million 
460:households were formed, roughly twice the pace observed in 
461:recent years and  well above the long-term average of 1.3 
462:million recorded from 1966 to 2007. 
463:Home prices have continued to rise, although the pace of 
464:increase has moderated from the rapid pace observed in mid-
465:2013. The FHFA purchase-only home price index rose 5.5 
466:percent over the year ending in August 2015, down from the 
467:July 2013 peak rate of 8.1 percent. The Standard and Poor’s 
468:(S&P)/Case-Shiller composite 20-city home price index rose 
469:5.1 percent over the year ending in August 2015, down from 
470:a peak of 13.7 percent in November 2013. Other house price 
471:measures show a similar pattern of decelerating home price 
472:appreciation. 
473:Growth of nonresidential fixed investment—about 13 
474:percent of GDP—grew by 2.1 percent at an annual rate in 
475:the third quarter of 2015, following a 4.1 percent increase in 
476:the second quarter. Growth of equipment investment 
477:accelerated to 5.3 percent in the third quarter from a modest 
478:0.3 percent gain in the previous quarter. In contrast, business 
479:spending on intellectual property products—including 
480:outlays for software, research and development, and 
481:entertainment, literary and artistic originals—slowed to a 1.8 
482:percent pace from 8.3 percent in the second quarter. In 
483:addition, business outlays for structures fell 4.0 percent. 
484:Altogether, nonresidential fixed investment added 0.3 
485:percentage point to real GDP growth in the third quarter, 
486:after making a 0.5 percentage point contribution in the 
487:second quarter. Finally, businesses accumulated inventories 
488:at a markedly slower pace in the third quarter following a 
489:substantial run-up earlier in the year. The resulting change in 
490:private inventories subtracted 1.4 percentage points from 
491:third-quarter real GDP growth. 
492:Exports account for about 13 percent of GDP, while 
493:imports (which are subtracted from total domestic spending 
494:to calculate GDP) account for just over 16 percent. In the 
495:third quarter of 2015, exports grew 1.9 percent. However, 
496:the small rise in exports was roughly offset by a 1.8 percent 
497:increase in imports. As a result, the net export deficit was 
498:little changed in the third quarter compared with its second-
499:quarter average and had a negligible impact on real GDP 
500:growth. Net exports added 0.2 percentage point to GDP 
501:growth in the second quarter after subtracting nearly 2 
502:percentage points from growth in the first quarter of 2015. 
503:The current account balance (reflecting international 
504:trade in goods and services as well as investment income 
505:flows and unilateral transfers) has been in deficit almost 
506:continuously since the early 1980s and in 2006 reached a 
507:record $807 billion, equivalent to 5.8 percent of GDP. The 
508:current account deficit narrowed sharply during the 
509:recession to $384 billion (2.6 percent of GDP) in 2009. It 
510:has widened somewhat since then but remains well below its 
511:2006 peak. In 2014, the current account deficit stood at $390 
512:billion, or 2.2 percent of GDP. In the second quarter of 2015, 
513:the current account deficit widened to $439 billion 
514:(annualized), or 2.5 percent of GDP. 
515:Government purchases—which account for about 18 
516:percent of GDP—have contributed modestly on net to 
517:economic growth thus far in 2015 after subtracting from 
518:GDP growth in each of the past 4 years. In the third quarter, 
519:government outlays advanced 1.7 percent at an annual rate 
520:after growing 2.6 percent in the second quarter. At the 
521:federal level, spending increased by 0.3 percent after a flat 
522:reading in the second quarter. State and local government 
523:spending rose by 2.6 percent following a 4.3 percent 
524:advance in the second quarter. State and local government 
525:spending declined for 14 straight quarters from the fourth 
526:quarter of 2009 through the first quarter of 2013-the longest 
527:period of falling expenditures at this level of government in 
528:postwar history-but has risen almost continuously since the 
529:first quarter of 2013. Similarly, spending cutbacks at the 
530:federal level restrained overall growth from 2011 through 
531:2014. 
532:Labor Markets 
533:During the recession (from December 2007 through June 
534:2009), the economy lost 7.4 million jobs. Job losses 
535:continued even after the recovery began, but in February 
536:2010 employment began to rise again. Since then, through 
537:October 2015, total nonfarm payroll employment has 
538:increased by 13.0 million. Private-sector employment has 
539:grown for 68 consecutive months, the longest string of 
540:increases on record, and has risen by almost 13.5 million. 
541:Job losses during the recession were spread broadly 
542:across most sectors but, with the resumption of job growth, 
543:all of these sectors have added jobs. Since the labor market 
544:recovery began in early 2010, payrolls in professional and 
545:business services have risen by nearly 3.4 million, and the 
546:leisure and hospitality industry’s employment has increased 
547:by almost 2.4 million through October 2015. Employment in 
548:the manufacturing sector has expanded by 864,000 since 
549:early 2010. A few sectors added jobs throughout the 
550:recession and still continue to hire new workers: since early 
551:2010, the health care and social assistance sector has added 
552:

556:an additional 2.1 million jobs. On a net basis, the 
557:government sector also added workers to payrolls during the 
558:recession, although payrolls began declining late in 2008, 
559:and 
560:trended

566:employment has increased since then but growth has been 
567:uneven. From early 2014 through October 2015, the 
568:government sector has added just 177,000 jobs. Most of the 
569:growth has occurred at the local level, with the addition of 
570:124,000 positions. Federal government employment has 
571:edged up just 2,000 during this period. 
572:The unemployment rate peaked in October 2009 at a 26-
573:year high of 10.0 percent—5.4 percentage points above the 
574:4.6 percent average that prevailed in 2006 and 2007, before 
575:the recession began. Since then, the unemployment rate has 
576:trended lower and in October 2015 stood at 5.0 percent. 
577:Broader measures of unemployment have also declined. The 
578:broadest measure, which includes workers who are 
579:underemployed as well as those who are only marginally 
580:attached to the labor force (the U-6 unemployment rate), has 
581:fallen from a record high of 17.1 percent in early 2010 to 9.8 
582:percent in October 2015. The U-6 unemployment rate is still 
583:above its pre-recession average of 8.3 percent. The 
584:percentage of the unemployed who have been out of work 
585:for 27 weeks or more also remains elevated relative to its 
586:pre-recession average. In October, 26.8 percent of 
587:unemployed workers were included in this category 
588:compared with readings around 17.5 percent before the 
589:recession. 
590:Inflation 
591:Headline and core inflation rates remained relatively low 
592:and stable, due in part to low energy prices. Headline 
593:consumer prices were unchanged over the 12 months ending 
594:in September 2015, after rising 1.7 percent over the same 
595:period a year earlier. Energy prices fell 18.4 percent in the 
596:year through September 2015, substantially more than the 
597:0.6 percent decline in the year through September 2014. 
598:Food prices rose 1.6 percent over the year through 
599:September 2015, slowing from the 3.0 percent increase over 
600:the 12 months ending in September 2014. On a 12-month 
601:basis, core consumer prices (a measure that excludes food 
602:and energy) rose 1.9 percent through September 2015, 
603:slightly faster than the 1.7 percent advance in the year 
604:through September 2014. Core inflation has been below 2 
605:percent since early 2013.

607:and early 2015. They trended higher in the spring and early 
608:summer but have generally declined since then and remain 
609:well below their year-earlier levels. The front-month futures 
610:price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil averaged 
611:$46.29 per barrel in October 2015, more than $38 below its 
612:October 2014 average. The retail price of regular gasoline 
613:averaged $2.23 per gallon in October 2015, 83 cents lower 
614:than in October 2014.

618:percent of GDP) in fiscal year 2014. The deficit has
